To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the AMI Small-Array observations of 14 dark nebulae show that there is excess emission with respect to lower-frequency observations in five of the sources, with three of these being definite and two probable.
the AMI Small-Array observations show five new possible detections of anomalous microwave emission, one of which (L675) is a definite detection.
we have detected five possible spinning dust components towards five of the fourteen dark nebulae in our sample.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of spinning dust emission in a sample of 14 Lynds nebulae, of which we have identified five sources with possible spinning dust emission, one of which is a new detection.
the search for anomalous microwave emission from spinning dust in the interstellar medium, and our results suggest that spinning dust emission is present in the interstellar clouds studied.
the detection and characterization of anomalous microwave emission from spinning dust grains in the interstellar medium.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the anomalous microwave emission is a plausible interpretation for three of our sources, L675, L1103, L1246, with a probability of 90 per cent.
there is evidence for spinning dust emission from three sources, and that the evidence is less strong for the other two sources.
the AMI data provide evidence for the existence of anomalous emission from spinning dust in five of the fourteen dark clouds surveyed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we find five sources of which one is already known, one is a definite detection, and three are probable detections, with the latter three being the most significant.
we find five sources which have anomalous excess emission at 17 GHz with α 18 17 =−1.0 ± 0.6, and we report one new detection and three new probable detection.
we have found one definite detection and four possible detections, which is in agreement with the results from the SCUBA survey of Visser, et al.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the AMI Small-Array observations have detected five new sources of anomalous microwave emission in the direction of Lynds dark clouds.

the AMI observations of the Lynds clouds are consistent with the presence of anomalous microwave emission from the spinning dust model, and that these detections are not due to radio counterparts to protostars or protoplanetary discs.

the spinning dust component is not limited to the well-studied dark nebulae L1780, L1789 and L1157, but that there is likely a population of smaller, less well-known, dark nebulae which also show evidence for spinning dust.
